title: An hour without the phone

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Shabbat, from a Hebrew root for stopping. Your line was a day off from making.

Where's your phone right now? If you're listening to this, probably in your hand. Fair enough. But think about the rest of the day. On the table at dinner. On the pillow at night. In your pocket on a walk, buzzing against your leg, or not buzzing, and you check anyway. A whole day off, like yesterday's Sabbath, can sound impossible from here. So don't start with a day. Start with sixty minutes, and a piece of furniture.
screen: `WHERE'S YOUR PHONE?` → `NOT A DAY. AN HOUR.` → `AN HOUR WITHOUT THE PHONE.`

segments.voice: In a 2017 study at the University of Texas, people did tests of attention and memory with their phone in one of three places: face down on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. Phones were silent the whole time. The people whose phones were in another room did best. The researchers called the effect brain drain: part of your mind stays busy not checking the phone. Later studies have found smaller or mixed effects, so hold it loosely. But the practical lesson is simple. Face down isn't away. Silent isn't away. Away is away. That's why the practice has a drawer in it. Out of sight works better than willpower, because you're not spending the hour resisting; the phone is just a little harder to reach. A modern movement took this straight from the Sabbath. In 2010, a Jewish nonprofit started a National Day of Unplugging, and writers and families since have kept what some call a tech sabbath: one day a week without screens. That's the destination this week. The usual advice is to start smaller than you think: one hour, an easy one, like a walk or cooking dinner, with the phone in a drawer or another room. If your hand reaches for your pocket a few times, that's the habit showing itself. Let the hand come back empty.
screen: `THREE PLACES FOR THE PHONE.` · `FACE DOWN ISN'T AWAY.` · `A TECH SABBATH.` · `START WITH ONE HOUR.` · then, large: `THE DRAWER.`

segments.voice: Picture the drawer, or the other room, and picture sliding the phone in and closing it. Notice what your body does: a small tightening, maybe, or relief. Then picture the hour itself, the room quiet, your hands free, and choose which hour of the day it will be.
Brain drain, the effect researchers found when part of the mind stays busy not checking a nearby phone. Today's word.
Your line: the drawer. Face down isn't away; away is away. That's day one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: People who keep a tech sabbath often start with one screen-free hour, putting the phone in a drawer or another room, and lengthen it over weeks toward an evening or a full day.
